issues.passage: After abandoning every piece she could play, she claimed a richer repertoire than before.
issues.why: "Richer repertoire" correctly means a larger stock of pieces she can perform; the speaker's false claim does not make the word itself wrong. A careful reader would accept the usage as valid English.

fix.correctPassage: The pianist expanded her repertoire to include modern jazz standards.
wrongPassages: They enlarged her repertoire by ensuring she could play nothing and held no roles.
His repertoire of expertise was defined as the complete absence of any skill he could perform.
Stagehands built the orchestra's repertoire each night only by sweeping the boards between numbers.

issues.passage: The committee treated his single unrehearsed remark as the full repertoire of his expertise.
issues.why: "Repertoire of his expertise" is natural correct use (stock of skills). The committee's unfair judgment does not make the word wrong; the sentence is valid English.

issues.passage: Proof of his complete innocence only strengthened claims of his culpability.
issues.why: "Claims of his culpability" correctly uses culpability = blameworthiness. A paradoxical epistemic claim does not make the word itself wrong; a careful reader would accept the usage.
